headline: tripura plans major expansion of public healthcare needs around 2500 more nurses kiran gitte
content: The Tripura government is drawing up plans to strengthen public healthcare by expanding infrastructure and addressing shortages of doctors, specialist physicians and nurses, as demand for advanced medical services increasingly moves beyond major referral hospitals to district and sub-divisional facilities. Health Secretary Kiran Gitte, speaking to journalists on Saturday, said expectations from the state’s healthcare system have changed considerably. People are now seeking sophisticated diagnostic and treatment facilities closer to home, putting additional pressure on the government to strengthen hospitals at different levels and ensure that new infrastructure is backed by adequate medical manpower. The scale of the staffing requirement is particularly evident in nursing services. The state currently has around 3,000 hospital beds, but according to the Health Secretary, approximately 2,500 additional nurses would be required to operate healthcare services at the desired staffing ratio. The government has already begun increasing sanctioned manpower. Gitte said the sanctioned strength of doctors at AGMC and GB Hospital, which earlier stood at around 300, has now been increased to approximately 630. Around 400 nursing posts, including contractual positions, have also recently been created. Despite this expansion, he acknowledged that a substantial shortage of nurses remains in the state healthcare system. Gitte outlined these developments in the backdrop of a review of Tripura’s healthcare system by a delegation from the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. For this year’s assessment, North Tripura and Gomati districts have been selected. The Central delegation spent eight consecutive days examining different levels of the state’s healthcare delivery system, ranging from sub-health centres, primary health centres and community health centres to the implementation of various programmes under the National Health Mission. Dr Piyush Singla was present as an observer.

headline: Mallikarjun Kharge Calls Delimitation Bill 'Threat' Ahead Of Special Session
content: Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge on Saturday launched a strong attack on the Central government over the revised Delimitation Bill, describing the proposed legislation as a major "threat" to democracy and accusing the BJP-led government of attempting to concentrate power in its own hands. The Bill was approved by the Union Cabinet on Friday and is proposed to be introduced in the special session of the Parliament commencing on November 30. Addressing reporters at 10 Rajaji Marg in New Delhi, Kharge said leaders of the INDIA bloc had come together and discussed the implications of the proposed Constitution amendment. आज INDIA bloc के Floor Leaders के साथ बैठक हुई। इस बैठक में हमने मिलकर तय किया कि मोदी सरकार जो Delimitation बिल लेकर आ रही है, वह लोकतंत्र के लिए बहुत बड़ा खतरा है। यह खतरा इसलिए है, क्योंकि BJP लोकतंत्र को ख़त्म कर, पूरी सत्ता हमेशा के लिए अपने हाथ में लेना चाहती है। https://t.co/hmCGnDGHtg He said that the Bill "being brought by the (Narendra) Modi government poses a very big threat to democracy".

headline: Law and order deteriorating, corruption at peak under Uttarakhand BJP govt: Congress
content: Dehradun, Nov 28 (PTI) Congress party’s Uttarakhand election campaign committee chairperson Pritam Singh on Saturday criticised the Pushkar Singh Dhami-led BJP government, alleging that law and order has deteriorated, crimes against women have risen and corruption is at its peak under its rule. Questioning the government on corruption, the Chakrata MLA said if Congress comes to power, the state will have a transparent and corruption-free government. He said the Dhami government’s report card, released ahead of the polls, deserved a zero. The ruling BJP released its 16-page “report card”, with Chief Minister Dhami claiming his government has fulfilled “70 per cent” of promises made in the 2022 polls. Singh said that there is a “huge difference” between the words and deeds of the BJP government. “The law-and-order situation is continuously deteriorating; be is dacoity, murders, crimes against women and even the penetration of drugs into households. The Ankita Bhandari case is a stark example of the government not being able to do justice to the law-and-order situation in the state,” Singh said.

headline: NCP (SP) has decided to back delimitation bill: sources; 'will vote as per conscience’, says party MP
content: Mumbai, Sharad Pawar-led NCP has decided to support the Constitution amendment bill on delimitation-linked women quota in Parliament, and party working president Supriya Sule conveyed this decision to its leaders during a recent meeting, sources claimed on Saturday.Separately, an NCP leader claimed that even though a whip has been issued to party MPs to attend the special Parliament sitting from November 30, the official stand of the party on delimitation hasn't been communicated to them.The 'secrecy' over the party's position on the issue prompted its MP Amar Kale, who represents the Wardha constituency in Maharashtra, to say, "I will vote on the floor of the Lok Sabha as per my conscience". Sule has so far not opened cards on the party's stand. On Friday, she said the party would first examine the draft legislation if it is brought for discussion in Parliament before making its position clear.During the meeting of NCP district presidents and leaders held in Mumbai on November 26, Sule sought their views, saying the party had decided to support the delimitation bill, the sources told PTI, adding that the party MPs were not present.The NCP has eight MPs, including Sule.The district presidents told Sule that they will abide by the decision of Sharad Pawar and the party leadership, the sources claimed.The meeting was convened by Maharashtra NCP president Shashikant Shinde to discuss the drought situation and mitigation measures.Separately, an NCP leader said on Saturday that even though a whip has been issued to the party MPs, the official party stand on delimitation hasn't been conveyed to them.He claimed that the party leadership hasn't sought the views of its MPs and also hasn't conveyed to them the official line."Last month, when Sharad Pawar saheb held a meeting on the drought situation, the last five to seven minutes of discussion were about delimitation, where some MPs aired their views. To which Supriya Sule said the issue would be discussed after the bill draft is made public. The draft was released yesterday , but still there is no word from the party leadership," the leader added.According to sources, the meeting held on Thursday witnessed a heated argument between Sule and NCP MLA Rohit Pawar over an upcoming tractor morcha the latter had announced to raise issues of farmers.As tempers flared, senior leader Jayant Patil intervened to calm down the Karjat-Jamkhed MLA, they said.Party sources present at the meeting said Rohit questioned Sule on why NCP leaders were being prevented from taking part in his upcoming tractor morcha to highlight the farm distress due to drought."Are you going to take action against those who come for the protest?" he said, according to sources.Sule replied by asking Rohit not to use the party logo and flag during the protest, they claimed.When Rohit said the tractor morcha is not a single-party event, Sule purportedly asked why he wanted NCP leaders and office-bearers to attend.Sources also claimed that the trigger for Rohit's outburst was NCP women's wing president Rohini Khadse announcing support for his agitation; however, Sule objected to her going against the party line.Khadse has been sacked from her post since then.A special sitting of Parliament has been convened from November 30. The Lok Sabha has been reconvened on November 30 and the Rajya Sabha on December 2.The sittings will conclude on December 3, subject to exigencies of government business.The Centre is set to introduce a fresh constitutional amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha on Monday to roll out one-third reservation for women by increasing each state and Union territory's seat allocation in the House and the strength of their legislative assemblies by 50 per cent, and freeze the revised allocations and boundaries until 2051.The Constitution Bill, 2026, slated for introduction in the Lok Sabha on Monday, seeks to raise the House's maximum strength to 850, with up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union territories. It also proposes to raise the ceiling on the size of a state Assembly from 500 to 650.The objective of the present Bill is to give immediate effect to one-third reservation for women, including women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States and the Union Territories, through a delimitation exercise, the Bill's Statement of Objects and Reasons says.It says the exercise shall provide for an increase of 50 per cent in the number of seats in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States and Union Territories, over and above the number of seats existing immediately before such delimitation.This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

headline: Karthigai Deepam lighting LIVE: No public entry allowed at disputed Deepathoon pillar, says CRPF ahead of lamp lighting
content: Karthigai Deepam lighting LIVE: CRPF IG Vikram on Saturday said no public entry would be permitted near the Thirupparankundram Deepam pillar “for now”, adding that the decision on access will be “communicated later.” Some devotees on Saturday pushed aside barricades and entered the pathway leading to the top of Thirupparankundram Hill amid restrictions on public access to the DeepathoonOnly a single group of 50 devotees have been permitted to climb the Thiruparankundram Hill to attend the lighting of the Deepam atop the stone pillar at 5 pm, news agency PTI reported.The ceremonial lamp, Karthigai Deepam, is expected to be lit at the disputed Deepathoon (stone pillar) atop the Thirupparankundram hill near Madurai, as per the directions of the Supreme Court.The Supreme Court on Friday came down heavily on the Tamil Nadu government and temple authorities over the failure to implement its November 20 order wherein it permitted the lighting of the Karthigai Deepam atop Deepathoon on November 24. It once again ordered the lighting on November 28 and issued contempt notice to Tamil Nadu's top officials.Preparations for Deepathoon lamp lightingPreparations are underway for the lamp lighting on the Thirupparankundram Hill, with with court-appointed receivers holding consultations with the temple's hereditary priests earlier to finalise the exact time for lighting the Deepam. The SC bench had on Friday suspended the temple's board of trustees and appointed former Madras high court judges Justices S Vaidyanathan and V Parthiban as receivers to oversee the ceremony's administration.The receivers are also coordinating security and crowd flow with the deployed Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) unit near the site, news agency PTI reported. Temporary infrastructure has been provided around the Deepathoon stone pillar ahead of the ceremony, with heavy CRPF security around it.After the arrival of the receivers, consultations regarding the muhurtham (timing) for carrying the sacred flame from the Uchipillaiyar Mandapam to light the Deepam at the Deepathoon were held. At the same time, temporary platforms and scaffolding were erected around the stone pillar to enable safe access for the priests and officials.

headline: ‘Pawar betrayed progressive ideology’: Congress, Sena (UBT) slam NCP (SP) over delimitation bill
content: With the Sharad Pawar-led NCP (SP) appearing set to support the delimitation bill, its Maha Vikas Aghadi (MVA) allies, the Congress and Shiv Sena (UBT), on Saturday launched a sharp attack on the party, accusing it of backstabbing, abandoning its ideological commitment and betraying Maharashtra's interests by aligning with the BJP-led Centre.On Saturday, NCP (SP) chose to stay away from the INDIA bloc’s discussion on its strategy against the Delimitation Bill that is likely to be placed in the upcoming special session of the Parliament commencing from November 30.Senior Congress leader Vijay Wadettiwar accused NCP (SP) chief Sharad Pawar of abandoning the progressive ideology that he championed throughout his political career, and alleged that the party was driven solely by the pursuit of power. Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut went further, accusing the NCP (SP) leadership of compromising Maharashtra's self-respect by strengthening the hands of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah. “Sharad Pawar’s history is one of stabbing people in the back, and the people of Maharashtra and the country are well aware of it. NCP (SP) was formed solely for the sake of power. The party cannot accept living without power," he slammed and added, "It is like a fish out of water. It has now been proven that the party has no ideology."He said that Pawar is 86 years old and has spent his entire life advocating progressive ideology. "I never imagined that a leader like him would join hands with communal and fundamentalist forces,” Wadettiwar said.The Congress legislative party chief also recalled how leaders across political parties had supported Pawar's election to the Rajya Sabha when he was 85, hoping that the ideologies of Mahatma Phule, Rajarshi Shahu Maharaj and Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar would be represented in the Upper House. He alleged that Pawar was now working towards undermining that very legacy.“After delimitation, when the situation in the country changes, a list of those responsible for weakening democracy will be drawn up, and Sharad Pawar's name will figure in it,” he alleged.He also questioned the argument that the NCP (SP) was considering supporting the Bill to prevent a split in the party, and alleged that the decision had been taken collectively by Pawar and his daughter, Supriya Sule. “Their only concern is power. They were born for power, and all they think about is acquiring power and holding on to it,” he said.Raut, meanwhile, questioned the NCP (SP)'s justification for backing the government, pointing out that its eight MPs had been elected with the support of MVA constituents, including the Congress and Shiv Sena (UBT), and not the BJP. He said the opposition alliance had defeated BJP candidates in nearly five of those eight constituencies.“If you take a unilateral decision and stand with the government, I do not think the people of Maharashtra will tolerate it,” Raut said, accusing the NCP (SP) leadership of forgetting the political circumstances in which its MPs had been elected.He also reminded the party of the role played by Modi and Shah in engineering the split in the undivided NCP and breaking the Pawar family, questioning why its leaders were now willing to align with the same leadership.“This amounts to mortgaging your self-respect. If you are going to side with the BJP to help it retain power, then the party must first apologise to Anil Deshmukh and Nawab Malik,” Raut said, referring to the two former NCP ministers who faced legal action during the Mahayuti government's first tenure.In his sharpest attack, Raut said the political move would amount to a betrayal of Maharashtra and its people.“Modi and Shah have, for some time now, pursued a policy of bringing Maharashtra to ruin. Strengthening their hands amounts to betraying Maharashtra and its people. It is a betrayal of the Marathi people, and we will not tolerate it,” he said.Raut, however, refrained from directly questioning Pawar's decision, citing his health and hospitalisation. Instead, he held Pawar's colleagues responsible for preserving his political legacy, alleging that those who had been groomed and elevated by the veteran leader were now compromising his ideology for power.“I feel his colleagues have betrayed him,” he said and questioned the NCP (SP)'s argument for supporting the Bill that it was necessary to prevent a split. Raut said the country and Maharashtra were more important than the survival of any political party.“Our party was split, wasn't it? Seven of our MPs were poached to secure support for this very delimitation exercise. Does that mean we went and fell at Amit Shah's feet? No. We continued to fight, and we are still fighting,” he said. Warning the NCP (SP) MPs against supporting the legislation, he said they would face political consequences. “If even one of these MPs votes in favour of the Modi-Shah government, or rather, against Maharashtra, I can assure you that none of them will be re-elected. This is not about voting against the government; it is about voting against Maharashtra. We will launch a massive agitation across the state,” Raut said.The remarks have come soon after it was clear that NCP (SP) will support the Delimitation Bill irrespective of its impact in its relation in the Opposition led INDIA bloc.

headline: NIA probing role of Myanmar-based ethnic armed groups, anti-India elements in terror acts in Manipur
content: New Delhi, The National Investigation Agency has opened a fresh investigation into the role of Myanmar-based ethnic armed organisations and other anti-India elements in alleged terrorist activities in Manipur, officials said on Saturday.They said these ethnic armed organisations are allegedly supplying arms, ammunition and explosives to proscribed and insurgent groups in India.The NIA has filed an FIR in this regard on the direction of the Union home ministry to unearth a larger conspiracy behind acts of terror in Manipur.The agency is already looking into the alleged involvement of US national Matthew Aaron Van Dyke and six Ukraine nationals in training ethnic armed groups in Myanmar. The seven were arrested by the NIA earlier this year on charges of illegally crossing over to Myanmar from India. The US national is currently out on default bail.According to the latest FIR, "certain ethnic armed organisations and other anti-India elements" operating from Myanmar, in criminal conspiracy with leadership and cadres of proscribed terrorist outfits and insurgent organisations like People's Liberation Army , People's Revolutionary Party of Kangleipak , People's Revolutionary Party of Kangleipak-Progressive , etc., are committing terrorist activities in Manipur.These organisations are also raising, providing and transmitting funds through clandestine channels, with the intent that such arms, ammunition, explosives and funds are used for the commission of terrorist acts within India, the FIR said.They are conspiring to commit terrorist acts, including targeted killings of innocent civilians and attacks upon security forces, with the aim of inflaming enmity and hatred between different ethnic communities in the region, provoking violence and displacement, and striking terror among the people, the FIR said.Manipur has been witnessing ethnic tensions since May 2023 between the Meitei and Kuki communities.The ethnic strife has so far claimed at least 306 lives, while 49 people remain missing and thousands homeless.This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

headline: Methil Radhakrishnan receives Ezhuthachan Award, Keralam’s highest literary honour
content: Kozhikode Methil Radhakrishnan introduced an experimental form of writing in Malayalam by easily blending science and philosophy with literature, Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan has said. He was delivering a speech after presenting Ezhuthachan Award, the highest literary honour given by the Kerala government, to Mr. Radhakrishnan at the Kozhikode Town Hall here on Saturday (November 28, 2026). https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/kerala/keralam-govts-ezhuthachan-award-for-methil-radhakrishnan/article71652290.ece Mr. Satheesan said that Mr. Radhakrishnan style of writing and presentation of language were original and thus different from others. “Bringing in science and philosophy in literature was considered a difficult proposition earlier. Mr. Radhakrishnan, one of the torch-bearers of post-modernism in Malayalam literature, proved that it was possible without the reader even noticing the process,” the Chief Minister said, adding that Mr. Radhakrishnan had also been a keen observer of nature, unlike many others, which get reflected in his writing as well. “The literary works of very few writers merit a re-reading. Mr. Radhakrishnan is one among them,” Mr. Satheesan pointed out. Kalpetta Narayanan, writer, described Mr. Radhakrishnan as someone who walked much ahead of his times, while deeply engaging with multiple subjects in his writing. Describing Ezhuthachan as a modern writer, Mr. Radhakrishnan said in his acceptance speech that the father of modern Malayalam language had been a formative influence in his literary career. Each letter in Ezhuchachan’s Harinamakeerthanam described a different human experience, Mr. Radhakrishnan said. Writer Sara Joseph, Minister for Cultural Affairs P.C. Vishnunadh, Kozhikode MP M.K. Raghavan, MLAs K. Praveenkumar and K. Jayanth, K. Gopalakrishnan, Special Secretary (Cultural Affairs), and District Collector M.S. Madhavikutty, among others, were present. The annual award, the highest literary honour in Keralam, is named after Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan, believed to be the father of modern Malayalam language. It comes with a ₹5 lakh reward and a citation.

headline: 'All MPs should support it rising above party lines': Suvendu Adhikari on delimitation Bill
content: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday urged all MPs to support the proposed women's reservation and delimitation-linked bills in Parliament, saying they should rise above party lines. He expressed confidence that the legislation would be passed with a two-thirds majority during the special session beginning November 30."The bills will be passed with a two-thirds majority," news agency PTI quoted Adhikari as saying."Everyone (MPs) should support the bills rising above party lines. Those who want the empowerment of our mothers and sisters will vote in favour of the bills,” he added.The Centre has convened a four-day special sitting of Parliament from November 30. It plans to introduce three bills, including a Constitution amendment, to implement 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies before the 2029 parliamentary elections. The proposed legislation also provides for a 50% increase in seats for each state.The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeks to raise the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha to 850. This would include up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union territories. It also proposes increasing the maximum strength of a state assembly from 500 to 650.The legislation links the implementation of women's reservation with the proposed expansion of legislatures and delimitation.Ahead of the special sitting, Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday said his government would remove every obstacle to implementing 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies.In a video message posted on X, PM Modi said the government remained committed to fulfilling its promise to the country's 'Nari Shakti'."Our resolve to empower 'Nari Shakti' remains unshaken. I want to assure every woman in the country that we will definitely eliminate and remove every obstacle that comes in the way of women's reservation," he said.The prime minister said those opposing the legislation would not be able to stop women's increased participation in Parliament and state assemblies."The parties opposing women's reservation will never be able to stop the country's 'Nari Shakti' from increasing their participation in Parliament and the state assemblies. It is just a matter of time," he said.PM Modi added that the supporters of the Bill were determined to see it through, saying, "our courage is unbreakable, and our resolve is steadfast".Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

headline: President recommends Lok Sabha to consider delimitation bill ahead of Parliament sitting
content: President Droupadi Murmu on Saturday recommended the Lok Sabha to consider the Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026 under Article 117(3) of the Constitution. The development comes ahead of the special Lok Sabha sitting from November 30 to December 3.A copy of the Bill, scheduled to be tabled in Lok Sabha during the special sitting, was accessed by HT after it was cleared by the Union Cabinet on Friday. It proposes to add 50% to every state’s and Union territory’s Lok Sabha seats, and to every assembly.The other bill - the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, says each state’s share of the Lok Sabha would remain the same till 2051. Follow live updates on the delimitation issue here.Both bills are due to be introduced in the Lok Sabha, which meets from Monday for a four-day special sitting. After the delimitation, the number of seats in Lok Sabha seats will increase up to 850, of which 815 will be from states and 35 from Union territories.Also Read: The population politics behind the 1976 freeze on number of Lok Sabha seatsWhat is Article 117 (3)?Article 117 of the Constitution deals with the special provisions relating to Financial Bills.According to Bar and Bench, Article 117 (3) pertains to a bill that “if enacted and brought into operation, would involve expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India”.Such bills cannot be passed by either House unless the President has recommended its consideration, the publication further said.Also Read: 50% more seats, bigger state assemblies: Five changes in the new delimitation billsInside the delimitation billsEach state’s share of Lok Sabha seats has been based on the 1971 census since 1976. Under the new bills, the state's Lok Sabha seat share will increase by 50%, which leaves the 1971 base in place.For every state, constituency boundaries will be redrawn using the latest available Census figures when the amendment comes into effect.Currently, constituency boundaries are based on the 2001 Census. Since the 2027 Census is still underway, the 2011 Census is likely to be the basis for redrawing constituency boundaries if the amendment comes into force and the delimitation process begins.Also Read: INDIA bloc races to consolidate Opposition against delimitation bill, may appeal to DMKBoth the seat numbers and the boundaries then stay in place until 2051. The existing freeze was due to end with the first census after 2026.

headline: Sabarimala priest urges pilgrims not to discard clothes in the Pampa
content: KOCHI Sabarimala Melsanthi Areekkara Subrahmanyan Sankaran Namboothiri has urged the pilgrims to stop discarding clothes in the Pampa, terming it an “ill custom”. In a statement to media on Saturday, the top priest highlighted the need to preserve the river which is a key part of the Sabarimala pilgrimage. “Everyone is aware of the need to keep the Pampa river clean and hygienic. Unhealthy practices such as discarding clothes in the river must be avoided. The Pampa river is like Mother Ganga. It is revered as Pampa Matha, and the river is associated with the concept of motherhood. It is the duty of every devotee of Lord Ayyappa to keep the river clean,” he said. He urged the pilgrims to strictly follow the instructions issued by the Travancore Devaswom Board and the police, and adhere to the concept treating the hill shrine as Lord Ayyappa’s Poonkavanam or sacred abode. He also requested devotees not to pack plastic articles in their irumudikettu, adding that these were among the most important things pilgrims should keep in mind. Recently, the authorities had decided to impose an on-the-spot fine of up to ₹5,000 on those found dumping used clothes and waste into the Pampa river during the ongoing Mandala-Makaravilakku season. Ends/Rg

headline: Andhra Pradesh DGP hands over ₹74 lakh financial aid to surrendered Maoists
content: VIJAYAWADA Director General of Police (DGP) Harish Kumar Gupta handed over ₹74 lakh towards Rehabilitation Assistance to the surrendered Maoists on Saturday. The DGP, along with Special Intelligence Branch (SIB) Inspector General of Police P.H.D. Ramakrishna and other officers distributed the Demand Drafts (DDs) to 18 Maoists, at the AP Police Headquarters, at Mangalagiri. Speaking on the occasion, Mr. Harish Kumar Gupta said that Rehabilitation Assistance would be provided to 32 more Maoists soon, who have joined in the mainstream in the last two years. Mr. Ramakrishna said ₹2.87 crore has been granted to 134 surrendered Maoists since 2025. Government will provide necessary support to the surrendered Maoists to reintegrate them into the mainstream. “I surrendered before the police and I am doing agriculture now. The Rehabilitation Policy being implemented by the Andhra Pradesh Police is good,” said Jagadeesh, who received ₹4 lakh financial aid from the DGP. DIG (Law and Order) K. Fakeerappa, SP Arif Hafeez, SP V. Geetha Devi and other officers also participated. //Ends.1245 Hrs.

headline: New Ludhiana Police Commissioner Satinder Singh assumes charge, vows zero tolerance towards crime
content: Newly appointed Ludhiana Police Commissioner Satinder Singh assumed charge on Saturday. He was warmly welcomed by police officers and personnel at the Police Commissionerate, where he was accorded a formal guard of honour.Speaking to mediapersons, Singh said the Chief Minister and the Director General of Police had given clear directions to make Punjab drug-free and crime-free. He said his top priority would be to crack down on drug trafficking and adopt a zero-tolerance approach towards all forms of crime.He said the Ludhiana police team was already performing well and that all officers and personnel would be encouraged to work to their full potential to achieve tangible results in making the city free of drugs and crime.Highlighting the sacrifices made by the Punjab Police, Singh said the force had played a crucial role in ending terrorism in the state, with several personnel laying down their lives in the line of duty. The police would continue to discharge their responsibilities with the same commitment, he added.He said the department had experienced officers and capable personnel, and that public cooperation would be crucial in further strengthening law and order. His endeavour would be to ensure that every citizen felt safe and continued to have faith in the police.Responding to questions about police personnel deployment at police stations and his future plans, Singh said he had just assumed charge and would first assess the existing systems and working arrangements. Necessary changes would be made wherever required to improve police functioning.He assured that the police force would work with dedication and focus on delivering tangible results on the ground rather than making mere assurances.

headline: A 1968 deal settled Mathura's temple-mosque dispute. Now, 58 years later, its validity is under fire
content: NEW DELHI: A compromise signed on October 12, 1968, was meant to settle a dispute over land in Mathura where the Lord Krishna Janmabhoomi temple and the Shahi Eidgah mosque stand today. It laid down boundaries, specified which portions were to be handed over to each side and sought to prevent future disputes over access and construction.Almost 58 years later, that agreement has emerged as one of the most consequential documents in the Krishna Janmabhoomi-Shahi Eidgah dispute. Hindu litigants contend that the organisation which entered into the settlement had no authority to compromise over property belonging to the deity. The Muslim side, meanwhile, has relied on the agreement and the civil court decrees that followed it to argue that the dispute had already been settled.The Allahabad high court has not delivered a final verdict on the validity of the 1968 compromise. On November 20, 2026, it dismissed an application seeking to declare the agreement "null and void" and cancel the decrees passed in 1973 and 1974. However, the court made it clear that the relief sought could not be decided through an interim application, as it was also the main relief in some connected suits and would require a trial.The dismissal, the court said, was without affecting the merits of the other suits. With the next hearing scheduled for December 10, the agreement remains at the centre of a dispute involving ownership, the authority of the parties who signed it and the legal protection available to places of worship.What led to the 1968 compromiseThe dispute concerns the Katra Keshav Dev complex in Mathura, with Hindu litigants claiming rights over a 13.37-acre property. The historical account of the site forms a significant part of the pleadings before the high court, though the claims about events centuries ago remain disputed.In its August 1, 2024 judgment, the Allahabad high court recorded the historical narrative advanced by the Hindu plaintiffs. According to their pleadings, a temple was built at the site in 1618 by Raja Veer Singh Bundela of Orchha. They alleged that Mughal ruler Aurangzeb partially demolished it in 1669-70 and raised a structure that came to be known as the Idgah mosque.The plaintiffs further stated that the British put 13.37 acres of land at Katra Keshav Dev up for public auction in 1815 and that Raja Patnimal of Benaras purchased it. His descendants later sold the property, with the transaction involving Seth Jugal Kishore Birla and the names of Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya, Goswami Ganesh Dutt and Bhiken Lalji Aattrey appearing in the land's subsequent history.The 2024 judgment also refers to a trust deed dated March 9, 1951, through which the entire 13.37-acre property was dedicated to the Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi Trust. The document stated that one of the trust's objectives was to construct a temple at the birthplace of Lord Krishna.A key distinction in the present dispute is between this trust and the Shri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sangh, the organisation that later entered into the 1968 compromise. The Hindu plaintiffs argue that the two were separate legal entities and that the Seva Sangh neither owned the property nor had the authority to enter into an agreement affecting the deity's rights.What did the agreement provideThe 1968 settlement arose from Civil Suit No. 43 of 1967, filed by the Shri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sangh against the Trust Shahi Masjid Idgah and others. The dispute also involved Muslim residents, including people described in the court record as Ghosis and other inhabitants who claimed to be tenants or licensees.The Allahabad high court's 2024 judgment records that the Idgah Trust had obtained permission from the Waqf Board through a letter dated September 9, 1968. A meeting held on October 8 that year adopted the agreement and authorised representatives to act on its behalf.The compromise was signed on October 12, 1968, presented before the court on October 17 and registered on November 22, according to the court record. The suit was eventually decreed on the basis of the compromise on July 20, 1973. A further decree followed on November 7, 1974.The agreement was not simply a broad understanding that both religious structures could continue to exist. It laid down specific arrangements for the land and physical boundaries between the two sides.Among other provisions, it required the northern and southern walls of the Idgah's "Kachchi Kursi" to be extended eastwards towards the railway line. The Idgah Trust was to get certain Muslim inhabitants living outside those walls vacated and hand over possession of the land to the Seva Sangh.It also dealt with land around the Idgah, including a portion on its western-northern side. The agreement provided for the removal of rubble from steps on the southern side, after which the Seva Sangh would take possession of the land.There were restrictions on construction facing the other side. The Trust was not to install doors, windows or grills in walls facing the Seva Sangh, or open drains or water outlets in that direction. The Seva Sangh was bound by similar restrictions. It was to divert water from the Idgah's outlets through pipes and construct a masonry drain at its own cost.The agreement further provided that both sides would file compromise applications in their pending cases after fulfilling the stipulated conditions. Either side could approach a court in the event of non-compliance.In effect, the document attempted to settle disputes over possession and the use of adjoining portions through a defined physical arrangement. It is this settlement, and whether the parties who signed it had the legal authority to do so, that is now being contested.Why is the agreement being challengedThe challenge rests substantially on the distinction between the Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi Trust and the Seva Sangh.The Hindu plaintiffs argue that the property had been vested in the Janmabhoomi Trust through the 1951 trust deed, while the Seva Sangh was a separate organisation. According to their pleadings, the Seva Sangh had no ownership rights and could not enter into a compromise affecting the interests of the deity.They also contend that neither the deity nor the Janmabhoomi Trust was a party to Civil Suit No. 43 of 1967 or the subsequent settlement. The plaintiffs argue that the Seva Sangh represented itself as having authority over the property and conceded land that it had no right to surrender.Advocate Kanu Agarwal told TOI, "The deity or the trust were never the parties to the Civil Suit No. 43 of 1967 or to the compromise deed dated 12.10.1968." He said the Seva Sangh was a distinct legal entity from the Janmabhoomi Trust and "prima facie was not the owner of the suit property".The 2024 high court judgment records these arguments, including the plaintiffs' claim that the compromise was fraudulent and that the decrees based on it should not bind the deity or devotees.The defendants have contested this position. The court record notes the argument that the compromise was entered into by recognised representatives, with the Idgah Trust having obtained the Waqf Board's permission. The Muslim side has also relied on the subsequent civil court decrees and argued that a challenge to the settlement cannot be brought through fresh proceedings.The central legal question, therefore, is whether the Seva Sangh had the authority to enter into the compromise, whether the settlement could bind the deity and the trust, and what legal effect should be given to the civil court decrees.How the dispute returned to courtThe current round of litigation gained momentum in 2020, when a suit was filed by advocate Ranjana Agnihotri and six others on behalf of the deity and devotees. The plaintiffs sought ownership of the 13.37-acre property, removal of the Shahi Eidgah structure and restoration of the temple.The suit challenged the 1968 compromise and the decrees passed in 1973 and 1974, arguing that the settlement could not extinguish the rights of the deity because neither the deity nor the Janmabhoomi Trust was a party to the original proceedings.The issue soon became part of a wider legal and political debate around the Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991, which bars conversion of the religious character of a place of worship as it existed on August 15, 1947, subject to the Act's provisions and exceptions.On the Places of Worship Act, Advocate Kanu Agarwal said, "The compromise deed of 1968 has no bearing or connection with Places of Worship Act."He added while talking to TOI that the site's religious character and title "would require detailed trial wherein evidence is led by the parties".In May 2022, AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi questioned the revival of the dispute, referring to the 1968 settlement. "Sri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sangh and the Shahi Idgah Trust had resolved their issues by an agreement in 1968," he tweeted, adding, "Why revive it now?" Owaisi also invoked the Places of Worship Act.The Hindu side, however, maintained that the agreement was not binding on the deity and that its validity needed to be examined by a court.What the HC has said so farOn August 1, 2024, the Allahabad high court rejected applications filed by the Muslim side seeking dismissal of the Hindu worshippers' suits at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.The court held that the suits could proceed and were not barred at that stage by the Places of Worship Act, the Waqf Act or the Limitation Act. This was a ruling on maintainability, not a final decision on ownership of the property or the validity of the 1968 agreement.The judgment examined arguments over the trust deed, the identity of the Seva Sangh, the original suit and the compromise. It observed that questions concerning the legality and validity of the agreement were factual issues that would require evidence during trial.The court's observations did not settle the dispute over title. Instead, they allowed the suits to move forward so that the competing claims could be examined through the judicial process.The litigation also moved to the question of a survey of the disputed premises. In December 2023, the high court had allowed an application seeking a court-monitored inspection. The Supreme Court stayed the implementation of that order in January 2024 in Special Leave Petition No. 481/2024.The survey issue remains linked to the Supreme Court proceedings. On November 21 that the high court had said it could not pass a fresh order on a similar survey application until the Supreme Court finally adjudicated the pending petition.November 20 order: No final ruling on the 1968 settlementThe latest development has again brought the compromise into focus.In an order dated November 20, 2026, Justice Avnish Saxena dealt with four applications in Original Suit No. 7 of 2023. One of them, Application No. 56Ga2, sought a declaration that the October 12, 1968 agreement was null and void, cancellation of the 1973 and 1974 decrees and delivery of vacant possession of the disputed premises to the deity.The court noted that the suit was among 18 matters concerning the same property. Since the relief sought through the application was also the principal relief in some connected suits, it said the issue could not be adjudicated without a trial.The application was dismissed, but the order expressly stated that this was without affecting the merits of the other suits and that the application had not been taken up on its merits.In other words, the high court did not uphold the 1968 agreement or declare it invalid through this order. The question remains open for adjudication in the connected proceedings.The high court also dealt with applications concerning the representation of the deity and the impleadment of additional parties. It dismissed a plea seeking to implead descendants of Thakur Keshav Dev, observing that the deity was already represented through a next friend and that the purpose of adding the applicants had not been adequately explained.The next hearing in the dispute is scheduled for December 10.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

headline: DMK to support Delimitation Bill as there is no loss for Tamil Nadu: A. Raja
content: CHENNAI The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), whose numbers in the Lok Sabha are crucial for the passage of the new Constitutional Amendment Bill (Delimitation Bill), will support it as it provides for a 50% increase in Lok Sabha seats and, according to the party, entails no loss for Tamil Nadu. The party added that the State’s existing share of 7.18% in the allocation of parliamentary constituencies will not be reduced, and that the Bill proposes an extension of the existing freeze on the inter-State distribution of Lok Sabha seats for another 25 years. https://www.thehindu.com/topic/dravida-munnetra-kazhagam/ Centre proposes freeze on Lok Sabha seat proportions for States until 2051 storyline 1 https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/tamil-nadu/ Explaining the resolution adopted at a meeting of party MPs chaired by DMK president M.K. Stalin, party MP A. Raja said the party had maintained a consistent position, whether in the Opposition or in government, and there had been no deviation from or departure from its stand. DMK MPs’ meeting demands fair delimitation based on 1971 census storyline 1 DMK MPs’ meeting demands fair delimitation based on 1971 census DMK MPs’ meeting demands fair delimitation based on 1971 census A resolution adopted at the meeting said the MPs would act with determination during the special session of Parliament to protect Tamil Nadu’s right to representation DMK MPs’ meeting demands fair delimitation based on 1971 census storyline 1 Asked why the DMK, which had consistently opposed the BJP, had decided to support the Bill, Mr. Raja said there was nothing wrong with supporting a measure if its provisions were consistent with the party’s position. “Our stand is that the 7.18% share should not be altered. It is being maintained. What is your problem? We have held the same position even when the Congress was with us. Can you say that the DMK and Mr. Stalin have departed from their position?” he asked. Constitution Amendment Bill: April to November what changed Constitution Amendment Bill: April to November what changed The revised Constitution amendment Bill closes legal loopholes, extends the population freeze to 2051 and narrows Parliament’s discretion on delimitation Constitution Amendment Bill: April to November what changed storyline 1 “We have taken a stand based on our earlier position, which was endorsed by the Congress, both inside and outside the Assembly. It is politically indecent to portray the DMK as having adopted a new position because it is no longer in an alliance with the Congress,” he said. Pointing out that Tamil Nadu had lost two seats during the 1971 delimitation, Mr. Raja said such a loss would not occur this time. “Tamil Nadu’s share will be 7.21% instead of 7.18%. There is no loss. We have been told that there are some problems and shortcomings in the Bill, and we have discussed them with our leader. We will hold discussions with political parties and suggest amendments wherever necessary. Our leader has left it to us to raise these issues in Parliament. He has also asked us to discuss them with the government to address our apprehensions,” he said. Lok Sabha seat freeze is no longer linked to population stabilisation Lok Sabha seat freeze is no longer linked to population stabilisation The distribution of seats based on 1971 Census continued for 50 years for the reason that a readjustment would adversely affect the proportion of States that stabilised population. Population stability was a stated objective of the government. That link between population stability and Lok Sabha share has been removed in the 132nd Constitutional Amendment Bill NEWS ANALYSIS Lok Sabha seat freeze is no longer linked to population stabilisation storyline 1 Mr. Raja said the DMK had consulted party lawyers and legal experts from other political parties and concluded that there would be no loss either to Tamil Nadu or to the country. He said that if the BJP government resorted to gerrymandering through the Bill, as alleged by Congress leader P. Chidambaram, to sideline Christians, Muslims, and other linguistic minorities and deny them their due representation, the DMK, as a friend of minorities, would take steps to prevent it and fight for their rights. Union Cabinet clears delimitation bill Union Cabinet clears delimitation bill A similar attempt by the government was rejected in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon session in April Union Cabinet clears delimitation bill storyline 1 Asked about Tamil Nadu’s share, Mr. Raja said no assurance was necessary as the provision had been included in the Bill itself.

headline: Nearly 1 in 2 Telangana kids aged 1-4 anaemic, state ranks fifth: NIN survey
content: HYDERABAD: Nearly one in two children aged 1-4 years in Telangana are anaemic, with the state ranking fifth in India in anaemia prevalence at 47.4%, higher than the national average of 41.8%, according to the ICMR-NIN's first-ever Diet and Biomarkers Survey of India (DABS-I), also known as SAMPADA (2023-25).Telangana has the fifth-highest prevalence of anaemia among the states listed in the survey, indicating a significant nutritional concern among young children. Andhra Pradesh recorded the highest prevalence at 57.5%, followed by Gujarat (56.5%), Chhattisgarh (55.6%) and Bihar (48.8%). Telangana's prevalence is also higher than that of Tamil Nadu (43.3%) and Karnataka (35.6%).Noting that the findings were a serious concern, experts highlighted that maternal anaemia is a key contributor to the high prevalence of anaemia among children aged 12-59 months, stressing the need to ensure adequate haemoglobin levels even before pregnancy."Early childhood anaemia can impair brain development, growth and learning. Prevention begins before pregnancy with healthy maternal haemoglobin, continues with a nutritious pregnancy diet and extends to iron-rich complementary foods and age-appropriate supplements for infants," said Dr Sivaranjini Santosh, a paediatrician. She added that regular deworming, a diverse diet rich in fruits and vegetables, and adequate folate intake were also important.During Telangana's most recent National Deworming Day (NDD) round in July 2026, the state covered 90.31 lakh children (93.29%) aged 1 to 19 years out of a total target of 96.81 lakh across all districts."Supplementation alone may not be sufficient unless children's diets provide a range of essential nutrients. Along with iron-rich foods, families should be encouraged to include foods containing vitamin B12 and folate. Identifying the underlying deficiency through appropriate testing is equally important," said Dr B Narahari, paediatrician and president of the Telangana Govt Doctors Association (TGGDA).Meanwhile, the survey found that anaemia prevalence in Telangana drops to 23.8% among children aged 5-9 years, compared with 31.3% nationally. Among adolescent girls, 43.6% are anaemic, while 54% of women aged 15-49 years have the condition. Adult men fare considerably better, with a prevalence of 12.5%, compared with the national average of 22%.The survey also assessed micronutrient deficiencies, including iron, vitamin B12 and folate.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news. headline: NHRC seeks report from Punjab Govt over ‘desecration’ of Nishan Sahib in Gurdaspur
content: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has taken cognisance of a complaint alleging desecration and disrespect of the sacred Nishan Sahib at Dalla Mallor village in Gurdaspur district of Punjab and sought an action taken report from the state government and police within two weeks.In a notice issued on November 27, the Commission directed the Punjab Chief Secretary and the Director General of Police to inquire into the allegations and submit a report for its consideration.According to the complaint, a local farmer, Sardar Mangal Singh Ji, had donated 10 marlas of his personal land for the construction of a Gurdwara Langar Hall. The Sikh congregation subsequently installed the Nishan Sahib in accordance with Sikh traditions and Gurmat Maryada.The complainants alleged that certain miscreants belonging to an opposing group, allegedly backed by political individuals and misusing government machinery, desecrated and disrespected the Nishan Sahib.The alleged incident has deeply hurt the religious sentiments of the Sikh community, the complaint stated, seeking urgent intervention to ensure communal harmony and religious freedom.The complaint called for a fair, impartial and thorough investigation, identification of those responsible and strict legal action against the guilty. It also sought preventive safeguards to ensure that Sikh religious symbols and sentiments are respected.The NHRC Bench, presided over by its member Priyank Kanoongo, observed that the allegations prima facie appeared to involve violations of human rights and took cognisance of the matter under Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.The Commission has asked the Punjab authorities to submit an action taken report within two weeks. It has also directed them to provide a certified copy of the order or application issued by the competent authority for removal of the Nishan Sahib structure.If no such order or application was issued, the authorities have been asked to submit a detailed report explaining how government machinery was deployed to remove the structure and what action has been taken in the matter.The NHRC has also directed that a copy of the report be sent to its registry by email for consideration.

headline: Gerrymandering is the new buzzword amid delimitation debate: What is it and why is opposition worried
content: What if a party could improve its chances of winning an election simply by redrawing the map? That's the fear driving the opposition's concerns over delimitation. As the Centre prepares to push its legislation, parties are warning that changing constituency boundaries could reshape electoral battles in the BJP's favour ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha polls. The concern has a name - gerrymandering. It means manipulating electoral boundaries to gain a political advantage.Also Read| No change in LS strength, 25-year seat protection: INDIA bloc's demands on delimitationThe concern goes beyond the number of MPs each state will send to Parliament. Even if states retain their existing share of Lok Sabha seats, redrawing boundaries within them could change which voters are grouped together, weaken established political strongholds and alter the outcome in individual constituencies. The opposition fears this could give the ruling party an advantage without changing a single vote or removing anyone from the electoral rolls.Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi has accused the BJP of seeking to redraw India's electoral map to its advantage ahead of the 2029 general elections. The concern is that even if states retain their existing relative share of Lok Sabha seats, the way constituencies are carved out within each state could influence which parties and communities have a greater chance of winning.What exactly is gerrymanderingIn simple terms, gerrymandering is the practice of drawing constituency boundaries in a way that helps one political party win more seats than its overall support among voters might otherwise allow.There are two common ways this can happen.Packing involves concentrating voters likely to support an opposing party into a small number of constituencies. This allows that party to win those seats by large margins but reduces its influence in neighbouring constituencies.Cracking involves splitting a group of voters across several constituencies so that they become a minority in each. This makes it harder for them to elect candidates representing their preferences.In both cases, no voter needs to be removed from the electoral rolls. The advantage comes from changing how voters are grouped geographically. A party can therefore win a larger share of seats without necessarily securing a corresponding increase in its overall vote share.Where did the term come fromThe word has its origins in the United States in 1812 and is a combination of the name of Massachusetts governor Elbridge Gerry and the word 'salamander'.Gerry signed a bill that redrew the state's senate electoral districts in a way that benefited his Democratic-Republican Party. One of the oddly shaped constituencies was compared to a salamander in a newspaper cartoon published by the Boston Gazette on March 26, 1812. The term 'Gerry-mander' was born.Gerry himself reportedly found the proposal 'highly disagreeable' and lost the next election. His party, however, retained control of the legislature.The term has since come to describe the use of electoral boundary changes as a political tool.Why is the opposition worried about delimitationDelimitation is not limited to deciding how many parliamentary seats a state should have. It also involves redrawing the boundaries of individual constituencies within states.The opposition's apprehension is that the second part of this exercise could be used to alter electoral arithmetic. By changing which areas and voters fall within a constituency, boundary changes can weaken established political strongholds, divide concentrated voter groups or bring together populations with different voting patterns.This is why the opposition argues that protecting the relative share of Lok Sabha seats allocated to states may not be enough. Even if the overall representation of a state remains unchanged, the distribution of voters across its constituencies could change significantly.The opposition has cited the delimitation exercises in Assam and Jammu and Kashmir to question how constituency boundaries may be redrawn. These examples have become part of its argument for greater transparency and safeguards. However, changes in constituency boundaries or their political consequences do not, by themselves, establish gerrymandering. That would require evidence of deliberate manipulation for electoral advantage.Assam: How boundary changes can alter electoral arithmeticAssam's 2023 delimitation offers an example of how redrawing constituency boundaries can change the political landscape without increasing the total number of seats or removing voters from electoral rolls.The exercise retained the state's 126 assembly seats but changed their distribution and boundaries. Barak Valley's tally fell from 15 to 13, while Barpeta went from eight constituencies to six. The Bodoland Territorial Region gained four seats, taking its total from 11 to 15.The reservation pattern also changed. SC-reserved seats increased from eight to nine and ST-reserved seats from 16 to 19. Goalpara West became an ST-reserved constituency, while Barpeta and Naoboicha were designated SC-reserved seats.The redrawing also altered the concentration of voters across constituencies. According to the figures cited in the delimitation analysis, the number of Muslim-dominated constituencies declined from around 35 to 24. This changed electoral arithmetic in areas where the Congress and the All India United Democratic Front (AIUDF) traditionally had a strong base.The exercise was officially aimed at improving representation and reducing disparities in constituency size. The gap between the smallest and largest constituencies, measured by electors, narrowed from 3.54 times to 3.15 times, though significant differences remained.The Assam example illustrates why the drawing of boundaries matters politically. A constituency can retain its name or number while its voter composition changes, potentially altering the parties and communities that have a decisive influence over its outcome. It does not, on its own, prove that the exercise was gerrymandered.Who decides constituency boundaries in IndiaThe task is assigned to a high-powered body called the Delimitation Commission. In India, such commissions have been constituted four times under the Delimitation Commission Acts — in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002.The commission's orders have the force of law and cannot be challenged in court. They come into effect on a date specified by the President. Copies are laid before Parliament and the state assemblies concerned, but these legislatures cannot modify the orders.This makes the composition, independence and working of the commission important to the current debate. The Opposition wants assurances that the process will be impartial and that constituency boundaries will not be drawn to benefit the party in power.Why the seat increase has not settled the debateThe Centre's proposed 50% increase in Lok Sabha seats and the assurance that states' existing relative share of seats will be protected address one part of the delimitation debate. But the opposition argues that the absolute difference in representation between states will also matter.Rajya Sabha Leader of Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge has said that retaining the present relative proportion of each state's seats for 25 years would address two of the opposition's concerns, but not its 'first and fundamental concern'."The proposed Constitution Amendment Bill has been unveiled. The 'freeze' for 25 years of the present relative proportion of each State to the total seats of the Lok Sabha will address two of our concerns. However, the Bill does not address the first and fundamental concern. While the relative proportion of each State to the total is important, absolute numbers also matter. The increase of 50% will increase the 'gap' between the Southern States and the other States. The 'gap' will increase from 413 to 620. The enlarged gap will overwhelm the number of MPs of the southern states," he said.The debate, therefore, has two connected but distinct dimensions - how parliamentary representation is distributed among states, and how constituency boundaries are drawn within them. While the first determines the number of MPs a state sends to the Lok Sabha, the second can influence who those MPs are and which voters help elect them.That is why the opposition's questions go beyond the increase in Lok Sabha seats. It wants clarity on the rules, the data and the safeguards governing the redrawing of India's electoral map. At the heart of the gerrymandering debate is a simple question - will delimitation merely redraw constituencies to reflect population and ensure fair representation, or could the new boundaries also reshape the electoral contest in favour of those in power?Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

headline: India continues US trade talks, eyes early 2027 rollout of EU FTA
content: India and the US continue to negotiate a trade deal based on an interim agreement of February 7, the commerce ministry said on Saturday, underscoring the government’s focus on utilising full potential of operational agreements and prepare industry for the next big deal with the European Union.The India-EU free trade agreement “is expected to come into effect in early 2027”, the ministry said in a statement amid ongoing official preparation for formal signing of the FTA by mid-December during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Brussels visit. Post-signing operationalisation of the deal is expected to take at least three-four months. Commerce and Industry minister Piyush Goyal on Friday said the India-EU FTA would come into effect by March or April next year. HT reported it on Saturday.“Under the India-European Union agreement, duties will end upon its entry into force for 70.4% of the EU’s tariff lines, covering 90.7% of India’s export value, with a further 20.3% of tariff lines being phased,” the ministry said in its Saturday statement.Giving details of ongoing trade negotiations with countries like the US, it said: “With the United States, a framework for an interim agreement was announced on 7 February 2026, and negotiations are ongoing.” On Friday, the commerce minister said: “The US trade deal is close to culmination. The process and pathway, which were always something which held back finalising the deal, is now taking some shape.”People close to development said, India would sign the proposed interim bilateral trade agreement (BTA) only after all types of tariff uncertainties are put to rest. As FTA is a long-term, legal commitment for mutual benefit all kinds of ambiguities, including tariff-related uncertainties must be adequately addressed before concluding a deal, they said requesting anonymity. India has time till January to reply on the United States Trade Representative’s recent findings on the Section 301 investigation, involving excess capacity. Besides that, suitable resolution of product-specific Section 232 actions is required. Although 100% duty on countries buying Russian oil under the Lindsey O. Graham Act is currently waived off, but some certainty on this is also required, they added.The office of the USTR on Wednesday proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods after an investigation into what it called structural excess capacity in manufacturing. The rate would fall to 17% if India reaches an agreement. That is a point below the 18% agreed in a framework for an interim deal in February, and below the 18% proposed for India’s export rivals such as Bangladesh, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, and Vietnam’s 20%. Exporters have questioned how much that edge is worth.The statement spoke about the sixth round of negotiations with Canada that was held from 11-20 November 2026, with the objective of securing an agreement that delivers tangible benefits to farmers, industries, businesses and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). Negotiations are also underway with Chile, Peru, Israel and the Eurasian Economic Union, as well as Mexico and other partners, the statement said.The ministry is on a campaign mode to prepare industry to take full benefit of FTAs India has signed so far and upcoming deals. It has organized outreach initiatives in Jaipur and Dehradun on Friday to familiarise exporters, entrepreneurs and MSMEs with opportunities arising from India’s FTAs and facilitate greater access to international markets.“Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Minister, Shri Piyush Goyal, had earlier noted the expanding market access available to Indian businesses through recent Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and urged Indian businesses to utilise the opportunities opened by these agreements. He had said that India’s preferential access to global markets, representing around USD 10 trillion in GDP until a few years ago, had expanded by an additional USD 60 trillion over the last four-and-a-half years, taking the total to approximately USD 70 trillion,” the statement said.With ongoing bilateral and multilateral trade engagements across eight to nine geographies, this was expected to expand to around $85 trillion, representing nearly 76% of global GDP, over the next year to year-and-a-half, it added.Addressing exporters during the session, commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal spoke about the significant opportunities created by India’s FTAs and emphasised the need for Indian exporters, particularly MSMEs, to proactively leverage preferential market access.He encouraged exporters to identify sector-specific opportunities in FTA partner countries, participate in international exhibitions, develop overseas supply chains and explore emerging avenues such as cross-border e-commerce. Referring to Rajasthan’s strengths in sectors such as gems and jewellery, textiles, handicrafts, furniture and minerals, Agrawal urged businesses to translate these strengths into increased export opportunities.He also outlined the interventions under the Export Promotion Mission (EPM), including support for export credit, international exhibitions, testing and certification, overseas warehousing and logistics, aimed at enhancing the competitiveness of Indian exporters.

headline: Youth killed after objecting to posts on death rumours
content: The Ludhiana police on Friday claimed to have arrested five persons in connection with the murder of a youth identified as Honey, alias Kalu. Pawan Kumar, a friend of the deceased who was accompanying him at the time of the attack, is critical and undergoing treatment at a hospital.According to the statement of Santosh Rani, mother of the deceased, her son had informed her on Thursday afternoon that some persons had created a WhatsApp group and were posting objectionable content about him. The persons named in her statement included Rahul, alias Golu, Prince, alias Lalla, Mani, Gaurav and Manjit.She alleged that Rahul had uploaded Honey’s photograph with the word “RIP” and was spreading rumours about his death. When Honey called Rahul, the latter allegedly abused him and threatened to kill him.Around five minutes later, Honey left home on his motorcycle (PB-10-JL-4469) with his friend Pawan Kumar. His mother followed them and reached Kali Mata Mandir in Bindra Colony, where she allegedly saw Rahul, Prince, Mani, Gaurav and some unidentified persons attacking her son.The accused were allegedly armed with sharp weapons, including kirpans and datars, as well as bricks and stones. When Santosh Rani raised the alarm, the accused allegedly abused her and fled from the spot in their vehicles.Following the incident, the police registered an FIR at the Daresi police station in Ludhiana.

headline: Ahead of Hornbill Festival, Nagaland Dedicated an Entire Morning to Cleaning Its Public Spaces
content: Imagine if, for one morning, shops in your neighbourhood remained closed, government employees stepped out of their offices, and residents came together to clean the roads, drains and public spaces they use every day. Advertisment On 13 November 2026, Nagaland organised exactly such an exercise across the state. Starting at 6 am, government employees, village councils, businesses, civil society groups and residents came together to clean their surroundings. Advertisment Add The Better India As A Trusted Source Shops and business establishments were directed to remain closed until noon to allow people to participate. The occasion? Preparations for the 27th Hornbill Festival, which begins on 1 December and brings visitors from across India and beyond to Nagaland. Advertisment Interestingly, the state government calls this exercise 'mass social work'. So, how did Nagaland bring together people across its towns and villages for a common cause? A morning dedicated to public spaces On 2 November, Nagaland's Home Department issued a notification outlining how the statewide clean-up would be organised. Nagaland's Hornbill preparations began with a morning when civic duty took precedence over everyday business. Photograph: ( Nagaland DIPR ) Advertisment Deputy Commissioners were tasked with identifying areas that needed cleaning and dividing responsibilities among government departments, municipal bodies, village councils and other organisations. Municipal and town councils were responsible for coordinating the work in urban areas, while village councils worked with local officials in rural areas. The government also planned for what would happen to the waste once it was collected. Departments were asked to arrange workers and trucks to transport waste and debris, working alongside district administrations and local bodies. Advertisment Each area could plan its clean-up according to its own needs. In Pughoboto, for instance, government offices, institutions, wards and villages were asked to clean their respective areas. Village councils and Village Development Boards helped organise participation, while heads of government offices were asked to submit reports with photographs of the work completed. From shopkeepers to students, everyone pitched in Across Nagaland, different groups of people took responsibility for the public spaces they shared. In the state capital, Kohima, government employees, municipal workers, ward authorities, civil society organisations and residents cleaned roadsides, drains and other public spaces. Chief Minister Neiphiu Rio also visited the Kohima Peace Memorial and Eco-Park to inspect the work. In Dimapur, government officials, local organisations and citizens participated in cleaning several locations. In Mon town, residents from all wards joined the exercise, coordinated by the municipal council and district administration. For Nagaland's Hornbill festival related cleanup, by noon, shops reopened. But the message of responsibility is meant to last beyond the festival itself. In Peren district, the clean-up brought together government employees, village councils, churches, student groups, businesses and residents across the district headquarters, Jalukie town and Ahthibung subdivision. The district administration also reported that the collected waste and debris were transported to designated disposal sites. This last step is particularly important. For any community clean-up to be effective, people need access to a system that ensures the waste they collect is properly disposed of. Across India, communities are finding their own ways to make this possible. From villagers establishing their own cleanliness rules in Odisha to women running a waste management cooperative in Tripura, these efforts show what people can achieve when they take collective responsibility for their surroundings. Beyond the 10 days of festivities Held at the Naga Heritage Village in Kisama, around 12 km from Kohima, the Hornbill Festival celebrates Nagaland's cultural heritage through music, food, traditional crafts and performances. This year, the festival will run from 1 to 10 December. Called 'mass social work', the statewide drive turned festival preparation into a collective civic responsibility. Called 'mass social work', the statewide drive turned festival preparation into a collective civic responsibility. While preparations for performances, food stalls and cultural events are underway, the state is also paying attention to the roads, public spaces and sanitation facilities that visitors and residents will use. In October, Chief Minister Rio urged villages to take responsibility for keeping roads clean, particularly highways passing through or near their areas. The government has also emphasised waste management and hygiene at the festival venue, including educating food-stall operators about these practices. Nagaland's statewide clean-up offers a practical example of how residents and local authorities can work together: identify spaces that need attention, divide responsibilities, involve local communities and arrange for waste disposal. As Nagaland prepares to welcome visitors this December, the roads, neighbourhoods and public spaces that people have worked together to clean will be part of that welcome. The next opportunity lies in carrying this collective effort beyond the ten days of the festival, keeping these spaces clean for the people who call Nagaland home throughout the year.
